name: Alpha-GPC
lead: Alpha-GPC (L-alpha-glycerylphosphorylcholine, or choline alfoscerate) is a choline-containing compound that serves as a source of choline for the synthesis of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and for cell membrane phospholipids [1]. It is sold as a dietary supplement in the United States, where a 2012 GRAS notice addressed its use as a choline source, and it is a prescription drug in some countries such as Italy for cognitive decline [1].

In appearance and physique communities it is discussed mainly as a sports-nutrition and focus supplement. The chains people describe run through training: acetylcholine supports the nerve-to-muscle signal and mental focus, so sharper concentration and stronger, more explosive sessions could mean better training over time and, eventually, a better physique. Some also note interest in a possible growth-hormone response, which has been investigated in small trials [1][7]. These are community and industry claims about performance, not appearance outcomes that studies have measured.

Most published human research dates from Italian multicentre studies in the 1990s in stroke, transient ischaemic attacks and dementia [3][4][6]; later reviews and meta-analyses pooled these trials [15][16]. More recent registered trials have examined it for cognition and athletic performance in healthy adults [7][8][9][10].
infobox: Dietary supplement; not FDA-approved as a drug [1]

subs.h: Use in physique and sports communities
paras: Alpha-GPC appears in pre-workout and 'nootropic' products and in forum training logs. A T Nation member's 2010 log described it as a form of choline that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and that people feel working within an hour to a few days [19]. A 2025 review of preparation methods and biological effects describes its high choline content (41 percent by weight), ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and bioactivity studies spanning cognitive dysfunction, cardiometabolic disorders, anti-aging and ergogenic effects [18]. A growth-hormone angle appears in registered trials that measured muscle power, GH levels and cognition together [7].

Trials registered in healthy people include a volleyball-player study of physical and cognitive performance, a trial of acute lower-body muscular performance, and studies of cognitive and sports performance in young adults [8][9][10][14].

In Italy and some other countries alpha-GPC is regulated as a prescription medicine for cognitive disorders; Grokipedia says it is not FDA-approved as a drug in the US [1]. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of choline alphoscerate for adult-onset cognitive dysfunction included seven randomized trials and one cohort study, and reported effects when combined with donepezil; the authors note discrepancies between countries on its approval and effectiveness [15]. A 2023 meta-analysis of choline-containing phospholipids in stroke, covering 15 studies, reported that choline alphoscerate improved neurological function and functional recovery on certain scales, while citicoline did not [16].

Rat studies in the early 1990s reported that oral alpha-GPC reversed scopolamine-induced amnesia and increased hippocampal acetylcholine synthesis and release [2][5]. Another rat study examined molecular mechanisms in young and aged animals, and a pharmacokinetic study tracked radiolabelled alpha-GPC in rats [11][12]. In healthy volunteers, a comparison of free plasma choline after intramuscular alpha-GPC and citicoline was published in 1992 [13].

Alpha-GPC has the molecular formula C8H20NO6P and a molecular weight of about 257 g/mol; it consists of a glycerol backbone joined to a phosphate group linked to choline, and it occurs in small amounts in nature and can be produced synthetically or derived from soy phosphatidylcholine, per Grokipedia [1]. A 2025 review notes its choline content of 41 percent by weight [18].

Grokipedia describes low adverse-event rates in the Italian stroke trial [1][3]. Labelling and regulation differ by country: prescription in Italy and some other markets, dietary supplement in the US [1].

Grokipedia attributes the first preparation to Erich Baer and Marvin Kates in 1948 and the first commercial availability to Italfarmaco in Italy in 1987 as a treatment for cognitive disorders, followed by supplement sales in the US from the 1990s and later sports-nutrition use [1].

An open Italian multicentre trial of 2,044 patients with recent stroke or transient ischaemic attack followed mental recovery with alpha-GPC, given by injection and then orally [3]. A randomised multicentre study of 126 patients with probable Alzheimer-type dementia compared alpha-GPC with acetyl-L-carnitine and reported improvements in most neuropsychological measures in alpha-GPC recipients [4]. A multicentre trial in vascular dementia compared alpha-GPC with cytosine diphosphocholine [6].

Registered trials in healthy adults have examined effects on muscle power, growth hormone and cognition, on physical and cognitive performance in volleyball players, and on cognitive performance and sports performance in young adults [7][8][9][10][14]. A growth-hormone outcome is relevant to height-related community interest, but results have not been reported. No published studies have measured alpha-GPC against facial or body appearance outcomes.

A 2023 review of choline supplements, including alpha-GPC, describes preclinical and clinical work on memory and cognitive function [17]. Grokipedia mentions a 2024 randomized crossover study in resistance-trained men that reported acute improvement on a Stroop test with no significant effect on physical performance [1].
Grokipedia describes alpha-GPC as sold over the counter in the US and included in sports-nutrition products [1].
In stack discussions on T Nation it is mentioned as a choline source; marketing emphasises focus, memory and training performance [1][19].

lore.intro: Alpha-GPC is discussed in training communities as a pre-workout choline source for focus and power output [19].

claims.claim: Alpha-GPC before training improves focus and lifting power.
claims.believers: Supplement users say it works within an hour to a few days and cite its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier [19].
claims.experts: Small registered trials in healthy adults have measured muscle power, cognition and performance; Grokipedia reports one randomized crossover study with a Stroop-test improvement but no significant effect on physical performance [1][7][8].

claims.claim: Alpha-GPC raises growth hormone, helping body composition.
claims.believers: Sports-nutrition marketing and some posters cite a growth-hormone response [1].
claims.experts: A registered trial measured GH levels alongside muscle power and cognition, with no results reported in the record; no study has tested appearance outcomes [7].

card.summary: A choline donor sold as a cognitive and sports supplement; no appearance outcome has been studied.
card.note: Human evidence is mainly older Italian studies in stroke and dementia; one 2024 trial lists growth hormone as an outcome.

quick.overview:
Alpha-GPC is a choline-containing compound used as a supplement, and as a prescription drug in some countries, to support acetylcholine synthesis. Older Italian trials studied it in stroke and dementia, and newer ones in cognition and athletic performance.
No trial has tested it for appearance, and it is not a topic in looksmaxxing discussions.
quick.mechanism: It supplies choline, a precursor of acetylcholine and of membrane phospholipids; rat studies reported raised hippocampal acetylcholine.
quick.risks: Grokipedia reports low adverse event rates in older Italian trials; detailed safety data are limited. It is sold as a supplement in the US and is not FDA-approved as a drug.

chain: Focus and muscle-activation effects reported around workouts
Better training quality over time, claimed to support strength and physique
angle.text: Lifters use alpha-GPC as a pre-workout choline source, reasoning that better focus and power output lead to better training. Small trials have looked at muscle power, growth hormone and cognition in healthy adults.
